kinds.d: Potassium aluminium mica mineral specimen: silvery sheets and books, plus chromium-green fuchsite.

x.d: Green chromium-rich muscovite.
Chromium-rich mica variety.
Vanadium-rich muscovite.
Large sheets of muscovite from pegmatites; Nellore, India has produced sheets up to 5 × 3 m.
Muscovite from Mt Mica, Maine, and other New England pegmatites.
Muscovite from Slyudyanka, near Lake Baikal.

kinds.d: Lithium mica mineral specimen: pink, purple or lilac scaly masses, the commonest lithium mineral.

x.d: Lepidolite from Brazil, often with tourmaline.
Lepidolite from the Tanco mine, Bernic Lake, Manitoba, also a source of rubidium.
Lepidolite from Madagascar.
Lepidolite from the Ural Mountains, Russia.

kinds.d: Dark mica group specimen (annite-phlogopite series): black to brown books and plates.

x.d: Large black biotite sheets; recorded crystals reach about 7 m² at Iveland, Norway.
Biotite from the lava of Mount Vesuvius.
Biotite crystals from Bancroft and Sudbury, Ontario.

kinds.d: Magnesium mica mineral specimen: brown to golden books, the largest single crystals known are phlogopite.

x.d: Phlogopite from the Lacey mine, Ontario, where a single crystal of about 330 tonnes was found.
Phlogopite from Franklin, New Jersey and Edwards, Pierrepont, St Lawrence County, New York.
Phlogopite from the Slyudyanka region, Lake Baikal.
Phlogopite from Perkin's Mills and Gatineau County, Quebec.

kinds.d: Magnesium chlorite mineral specimen: green platy crystals; seraphinite is a decorative variety.

x.d: Massive compact clinochlore with feathery silver-green sheen, from the Korshunovskoye deposit, Irkutsk, Russia; used for carving.
Variety of clinochlore.
Clinochlore from the Zillertal, Tirol and the Ala Valley, Piedmont.
Clinochlore from the Tilly Foster mine, Brewster, New York.
Quartz with chlorite inclusions from Minas Gerais, Brazil.

kinds.d: Hydrated magnesium silicate, Mohs 1: the softest mineral; soapstone is the massive carving rock.

x.d: Coarse grey-green high-talc rock used for stoves, sinks, carvings and lab tops.
Talc from the Trimouns deposit near Luzenac, Ariège, France.
Talc from Mount Seabrook, Western Australia.
Talc from Mt Greiner, Zermatt and the Pfitschtal.

kinds.d: Serpentine-group specimen (antigorite, lizardite, chrysotile): green to yellow carving and ornamental stones.

x.d: Apple-green antigorite, hardness about 5.5, used for carving and jewellery; Rhode Island state mineral.
Oil-green antigorite with black chromite or magnetite inclusions, mainly from Maryland and Pennsylvania.
Green serpentinite marble from Connemara, Ireland, used as decorative stone.
Fibrous serpentine, a major asbestos mineral; handle with care.
Platy low-temperature serpentine, hardness about 2.5.
Serpentinite from The Lizard, Cornwall.

notes: All 7 planned kinds kept. Sources: Wikipedia and HOM (muscovite, phlogopite, clinochlore, talc). HOM has no lepidolite/biotite/serpentine file used. Kämmererite and leuchtenbergite not on the fetched clinochlore page so omitted; sericite not covered. No brands or traditions.
